All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

3	The infimum is
4	\[
5	\boxed{\frac19}.
6	\]
7	
8	I will prove both directions:
9	
10	* if \(c>1/9\), a finite triangle-free target exists;
11	* if \(c<1/9\), no finite triangle-free target works.
12	
13	The distinction between the forbidden cycles in the source and the target matters here: the target below is guaranteed to be triangle-free, but need not be \(C_5\)-free.
14	
15	## 1. Preliminaries
16	
17	A **walk** may repeat vertices and edges. In a simple graph, a closed odd walk of length at most \(5\) contains a triangle or a \(5\)-cycle. Consequently, throughout a \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph:
18	
19	\[
20	\text{there is no closed walk of length }3\text{ or }5. \tag{1}
21	\]
22	
23	Call a vertex set \(D\) **wide** if no walk of length \(3\) has both endpoints in \(D\). Such a set is independent: an edge \(uv\) gives the walk \(u,v,u,v\).
24	
25	Here is a useful source of wide sets. For any nonempty vertex set \(U\), put
26	\[
27	D(U)=\{x:|N(x)\cap U|>|U|/2\}.
28	\]
29	Then \(D(U)\) is wide. Indeed, if a \(3\)-walk joined \(x,y\in D(U)\), their neighborhoods would have a common vertex in \(U\). Appending the resulting \(2\)-walk from \(y\) to \(x\) would give a closed \(5\)-walk, contrary to (1).
30	
31	We use two classical theorems, stated precisely here.
32	
33	**Kneser’s theorem.** For \(N\ge 2k\), the graph \(KG(N,k)\), whose vertices are the \(k\)-subsets of \([N]\), with disjoint sets adjacent, satisfies
34	\[
35	\chi(KG(N,k))=N-2k+2.
36	\]
37	
38	**Degree-form regularity lemma.** Given \(\varepsilon,d>0\) and a positive integer \(k_0\), there are \(K,n_0\) such that every graph \(G\) on \(n\ge n_0\) vertices has a partition
39	\[
40	V(G)=V_0\sqcup V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k
41	\]
42	and a spanning subgraph \(G'\subseteq G\) such that:
43	
44	* \(k_0\le k\le K\), \(|V_0|\le\varepsilon n\), and \(|V_1|=\cdots=|V_k|=m\);
45	* \(G'[V_i]\) is empty for \(i\ge1\);
46	* each pair \((V_i,V_j)\), \(1\le i<j\le k\), is either empty in \(G'\), or is \(\varepsilon\)-regular in \(G'\) with density at least \(d\);
47	* \(d_{G'}(v)\ge d_G(v)-(d+\varepsilon)n\) for every vertex \(v\).
48	
49	These are the only general theorems needed.
50	
51	## 2. Lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails
52	
53	Fix \(c<1/9\), and let \(H\) be any finite triangle-free graph. Write \(h=|V(H)|\). An empty \(H\) plainly cannot work, so assume \(h\ge1\).
54	
55	Choose \(k\) sufficiently large that, with \(N=2k+h\),
56	\[
57	c<\frac{k}{3(N+k)}=\frac{k}{9k+3h}. \tag{2}
58	\]
59	Let
60	\[
61	F=KG(N,k).
62	\]
63	Kneser’s theorem gives
64	\[
65	\chi(F)=h+2>h. \tag{3}
66	\]
67	
68	### 2.1 A subdivided core
69	
70	Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace each oriented edge \(u\to v\) by the path
71	\[
72	u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v.
73	\]
74	Call the resulting graph \(S\).
75	
76	Give its vertices types and labels as follows. Labels are \(k\)-subsets of \([N]\).
77	
78	\[
79	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
80	\text{vertex}&\text{type}&\text{label}\\ \hline
81	u\in V(F)&0&u\\
82	a_{uv}&1&u\\
83	b_{uv}&2&v
84	\end{array}
85	\]
86	
87	The types form a proper \(3\)-coloring of \(S\). Also, \(S\) has no cycle shorter than \(9\).
88	
89	We need one additional fact:
90	\[
91	\begin{gathered}
92	\text{If a \(3\)-walk in \(S\) has endpoints of the same type,}\\
93	\text{then the labels of its endpoints are disjoint.}
94	\end{gathered} \tag{4}
95	\]
96	
97	For type \(0\), such a walk traverses a subdivided edge of \(F\), so its endpoint labels are adjacent in \(F\).
98	
99	For type \(1\), the possible walks, up to reversal, have the forms
100	\[
101	a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v-a_{vw}
102	\quad\text{or}\quad
103	a_{uv}-u-b_{wu}-a_{wu}.
104	\]
105	Their endpoint labels are respectively \(u,v\) or \(u,w\), which are adjacent in \(F\). Type \(2\) is symmetric. This proves (4).
106	
107	### 2.2 Add three reservoirs
108	
109	For a positive integer \(t\), and for each \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\), create
110	\[
111	A_i=[N]\times[t],
112	\qquad
113	B_i=[k]\times[t].
114	\]
115	Use separate copies for the three values of \(i\).
116	
117	Add all edges between \(A_i\) and \(B_i\). A core vertex \(x\) of type \(i\), with label \(L(x)\), is joined to precisely
118	\[
119	\{(r,s)\in A_i:r\in L(x),\ s\in[t]\}.
120	\]
121	There are no other new edges. Denote the resulting graph by \(G_t\).
122	
123	Every core vertex has \(kt\) reservoir neighbors. Every vertex in \(A_i\) has all \(kt\) vertices of \(B_i\) as neighbors, and every vertex in \(B_i\) has \(Nt\) neighbors. Thus
124	\[
125	\delta(G_t)\ge kt,
126	\qquad
127	|V(G_t)|=|V(S)|+3(N+k)t. \tag{5}
128	\]
129	By (2), sufficiently large \(t\) gives
130	\[
131	\delta(G_t)\ge c|V(G_t)|. \tag{6}
132	\]
133	
134	### 2.3 Verify the forbidden cycles
135	
136	There is no triangle:
137	
138	* the core has none;
139	* a vertex in \(B_i\) has an independent neighborhood \(A_i\);
140	* a triangle using a vertex of \(A_i\), but no \(B_i\), would require adjacent core vertices of the same type.
141	
142	Now suppose there were a \(5\)-cycle.
143	
144	If it used a vertex of \(B_i\), it would contain a segment \(A_i-B_i-A_i\). The remaining \(3\)-edge path between these two \(A_i\)-vertices would have to use an edge between core vertices of type \(i\), which is impossible.
145	
146	Assume therefore that it uses no \(B_i\).
147	
148	* With no \(A_i\)-vertex, it lies in the core, which has girth at least \(9\).
149	* With exactly one \(A_i\)-vertex, its remaining part is a \(3\)-walk in the core between vertices of type \(i\). Their labels are disjoint by (4), so they cannot have this common \(A_i\)-neighbor.
150	* With two \(A\)-vertices, the core vertex between them forces both to belong to the same \(A_i\). The remaining core edge then has endpoints of type \(i\), again impossible.
151	
152	Thus \(G_t\) contains neither a triangle nor a \(5\)-cycle.
153	
154	### 2.4 It cannot map to \(H\)
155	
156	Suppose \(f:G_t\to H\) were a homomorphism. Restrict \(f\) to the original vertices of \(F\).
157	
158	For each \(uv\in E(F)\), the subdivided edge is a \(3\)-walk from \(u\) to \(v\). If \(f(u)=f(v)\), its image would be a closed \(3\)-walk in \(H\), and hence a triangle. Therefore \(f(u)\ne f(v)\).
159	
160	So this restriction is a proper coloring of \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors, contradicting (3).
161	
162	Since \(H\) was arbitrary, every \(c<1/9\) fails.
163	
164	## 3. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
165	
166	Fix \(c>1/9\). Choose small \(d,\varepsilon>0\) such that
167	\[
168	d>\varepsilon,\qquad
169	c-d-2\varepsilon>0,\qquad
170	9c-3d-24\varepsilon>1. \tag{7}
171	\]
172	For example, with \(g=c-1/9\), take \(d=g\) and \(\varepsilon=g/100\).
173	
174	Let \(G\) be \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free with
175	\[
176	\delta(G)\ge cn.
177	\]
178	For sufficiently large \(n\), apply degree-form regularity.
179	
180	Let \(R\) be the reduced graph on \([k]\): \(ij\in E(R)\) precisely when the corresponding pair in \(G'\) is nonempty and regular with density at least \(d\).
181	
182	For any \(v\in V_i\),
183	\[
184	d_{G'}(v)\le |V_0|+m\,d_R(i).
185	\]
186	Consequently,
187	\[
188	m\delta(R)\ge(c-d-2\varepsilon)n>0. \tag{8}
189	\]
190	In particular, \(R\) has no isolated vertices.
191	
192	For a vertex \(x\in V(G)\), define its support
193	\[
194	A(x)=\{i\in[k]:|N_G(x)\cap V_i|\ge2\varepsilon m\}. \tag{9}
195	\]
196	
197	### 3.1 Three consequences of regularity and the forbidden cycles
198	
199	We will use:
200	\[
201	\begin{array}{ll}
202	\text{(a)}&A(x)\text{ is independent in }R;\\[2mm]
203	\text{(b)}&xy\in E(G)\Longrightarrow
204	N_R(A(x))\cap N_R(A(y))=\varnothing
205	\text{ and }A(x)\cap A(y)=\varnothing;\\[2mm]
206	\text{(c)}&x-y-z\text{ a \(2\)-edge path}\Longrightarrow
207	E_R(A(x),A(z))=\varnothing.
208	\end{array} \tag{10}
209	\]
210	
211	Here \(E_R(P,Q)=\varnothing\) means no edge of \(R\) has one endpoint in \(P\) and the other in \(Q\).
212	
213	For clarity, these implications follow directly from the definition of regularity. In an \(\varepsilon\)-regular pair of density at least \(d>\varepsilon\):
214	
215	* two subsets, one on either side and each of size at least \(2\varepsilon m\), have an edge between them;
216	* for a subset of size at least \(2\varepsilon m\) on one side, all but at most \(\varepsilon m\) vertices on the other side have a neighbor in it.
217	
218	Thus:
219	
220	* an edge inside \(A(x)\) would produce a triangle through \(x\), proving (a);
221	* a common reduced neighbor of \(A(x)\) and \(A(y)\) produces a walk
222	  \[
223	  x-a-r-b-y.
224	  \]
225	  If \(xy\) is an edge, this closes to a \(5\)-walk, proving the first assertion of (b);
226	* if \(A(x)\cap A(y)\ne\varnothing\), a neighbor in \(R\) of an index in that intersection is a common reduced neighbor. Such a neighbor exists by (8). This proves the other assertion of (b);
227	* an edge between \(A(x)\) and \(A(z)\), together with \(x-y-z\), produces a closed \(5\)-walk, proving (c).
228	
229	Repeated vertices cause no difficulty: (1) excludes closed odd walks, not just injective cycles.
230	
231	### 3.2 Remove boundedly many wide classes
232	
233	For every \(i\), the set
234	\[
235	\{x:|N_G(x)\cap V_i|>m/2\}
236	\]
237	is wide, by the preliminary observation.
238	
239	Assign every vertex satisfying one or more of these inequalities to the first such index. This gives disjoint wide classes
240	\[
241	D_1,\ldots,D_k,
242	\]
243	some possibly empty. Call their vertices special.
244	
245	For each remaining vertex \(x\),
246	\[
247	|N_G(x)\cap V_i|\le m/2
248	\quad\text{for every }i.
249	\]
250	Using (9),
251	\[
252	\begin{aligned}
253	cn
254	&\le d_G(x)\\
255	&\le |V_0|+|A(x)|\,\frac m2+2\varepsilon km\\
256	&\le3\varepsilon n+|A(x)|\,\frac m2.
257	\end{aligned}
258	\]
259	Hence
260	\[
261	m|A(x)|\ge2(c-3\varepsilon)n. \tag{11}
262	\]
263	In particular, \(A(x)\ne\varnothing\).
264	
265	Partition all nonspecial vertices according to their support \(A(x)\). Together with the nonempty \(D_i\), these form a base partition with at most
266	\[
267	p=k+2^k \tag{12}
268	\]
269	classes.
270	
271	Every base class is independent. This is already true for the \(D_i\); for a support class it follows from (10b) and the nonemptiness of the support.
272	
273	### 3.3 Refine by neighbor signatures
274	
275	Refine each base class according to the set of base classes in which a vertex has at least one neighbor.
276	
277	There are at most
278	\[
279	p2^p \tag{13}
280	\]
281	refined classes.
282	
283	Let \(Q\) be their quotient graph: two distinct refined classes are adjacent if some edge of \(G\) joins them. Since base classes are independent, this is a loopless graph, and the class map is a homomorphism \(G\to Q\).
284	
285	I claim that \(Q\) is triangle-free.
286	
287	Suppose its refined classes \(X,Y,Z\) formed a triangle.
288	
289	**First suppose that \(X\) lies in a special base class \(D_i\).** Choose an actual edge \(yz\) between \(Y\) and \(Z\). Because signatures are constant on refined classes, both \(y\) and \(z\) have a neighbor in \(D_i\). Thus there is a \(3\)-walk with both endpoints in \(D_i\), contradicting its wideness.
290	
291	**Now suppose all three classes are nonspecial.** Write their supports as \(A,B,C\).
292	
293	By (10b), the sets \(A,B,C\) are pairwise disjoint, as are
294	\[
295	N_R(A),\quad N_R(B),\quad N_R(C). \tag{14}
296	\]
297	
298	The neighbor-signature refinement also ensures that a vertex in \(X\) has a neighbor of support \(B\) and a neighbor of support \(C\). Applying (10c) to this \(2\)-edge path shows that \(B\) and \(C\) are anticomplete in \(R\). Cyclically, \(A,B,C\) are pairwise anticomplete. Each is itself independent by (10a).
299	
300	It follows that these six sets are pairwise disjoint:
301	\[
302	A,\ B,\ C,\ N_R(A),\ N_R(B),\ N_R(C). \tag{15}
303	\]
304	
305	Each of the first three has, by (11), size times \(m\) at least \(2(c-3\varepsilon)n\). Each of the last three has, by nonemptiness and (8), size times \(m\) at least \((c-d-2\varepsilon)n\). Therefore
306	\[
307	\begin{aligned}
308	km
309	&\ge m\bigl(
310	|A|+|B|+|C|+
311	|N_R(A)|+|N_R(B)|+|N_R(C)|
312	\bigr)\\
313	&\ge
314	3\bigl(2(c-3\varepsilon)+(c-d-2\varepsilon)\bigr)n\\
315	&=(9c-3d-24\varepsilon)n\\
316	&>n,
317	\end{aligned}
318	\]
319	contradicting \(km\le n\).
320	
321	This proves that \(Q\) is triangle-free.
322	
323	### 3.4 One target works for all inputs
324	
325	Regularity bounds \(k\) by a constant \(K\) depending only on \(c\). Hence (12)–(13) bound \(|V(Q)|\) by a constant depending only on \(c\).
326	
327	Choose an integer \(M\) at least this bound and at least the regularity threshold \(n_0\). Let \(H_c\) be the disjoint union of one copy of every triangle-free graph on at most \(M\) vertices.
328	
329	This is a finite triangle-free graph.
330	
331	* Large input graphs map to their triangle-free quotient \(Q\), which appears in \(H_c\).
332	* Every smaller input graph is itself triangle-free and appears in \(H_c\).
333	
334	Thus every \(c>1/9\) has the required property.
335	
336	Combining the two halves establishes the claimed infimum.
337	
338	## 4. Executed Python checks
339	
340	The following code performs genuine checks, rather than merely printing the proposed answer. It:
341	
342	1. checks the wide-set assertions on every \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph of order at most seven;
343	2. constructs explicit lower-bound graphs and checks the absence of triangles and \(5\)-cycles;
344	3. checks small Kneser chromatic numbers with Z3;
345	4. checks the core’s same-type \(3\)-walk label condition;
346	5. checks the six-set packing implication with Z3;
347	6. verifies exact lower-bound parameter arithmetic for implicit examples approaching \(1/9\).
348	
349	The infinite arguments are proved above; finite experiments are not being substituted for the regularity lemma or Kneser’s theorem.

364	\[
365	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
366	\text{vertex}&\text{type}&\text{label}\\ \hline
367	u\in V(F)&0&u\\
368	a_{uv}&1&u\\
369	b_{uv}&2&v
370	\end{array}
371	\]
372	
373	The types form a proper \(3\)-coloring of \(S\). Also, \(S\) has no cycle shorter than \(9\).
374	
375	We need one additional fact:
376	\[
377	\begin{gathered}
378	\text{If a \(3\)-walk in \(S\) has endpoints of the same type,}\\
379	\text{then the labels of its endpoints are disjoint.}
380	\end{gathered} \tag{4}
381	\]
382	
383	For type \(0\), such a walk traverses a subdivided edge of \(F\), so its endpoint labels are adjacent in \(F\).
384	
385	For type \(1\), the possible walks, up to reversal, have the forms
386	\[
387	a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v-a_{vw}
388	\quad\text{or}\quad
389	a_{uv}-u-b_{wu}-a_{wu}.
390	\]
391	Their endpoint labels are respectively \(u,v\) or \(u,w\), which are adjacent in \(F\). Type \(2\) is symmetric. This proves (4).
392	
393	### 2.2 Add three reservoirs
394	
395	For a positive integer \(t\), and for each \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\), create
396	\[
397	A_i=[N]\times[t],
398	\qquad
399	B_i=[k]\times[t].
400	\]
401	Use separate copies for the three values of \(i\).
402	
403	Add all edges between \(A_i\) and \(B_i\). A core vertex \(x\) of type \(i\), with label \(L(x)\), is joined to precisely
404	\[
405	\{(r,s)\in A_i:r\in L(x),\ s\in[t]\}.
406	\]
407	There are no other new edges. Denote the resulting graph by \(G_t\).
408	
409	Every core vertex has \(kt\) reservoir neighbors. Every vertex in \(A_i\) has all \(kt\) vertices of \(B_i\) as neighbors, and every vertex in \(B_i\) has \(Nt\) neighbors. Thus
410	\[
411	\delta(G_t)\ge kt,
412	\qquad
413	|V(G_t)|=|V(S)|+3(N+k)t. \tag{5}
414	\]
415	By (2), sufficiently large \(t\) gives
416	\[
417	\delta(G_t)\ge c|V(G_t)|. \tag{6}
418	\]
419	
420	### 2.3 Verify the forbidden cycles
421	
422	There is no triangle:
423	
424	* the core has none;
425	* a vertex in \(B_i\) has an independent neighborhood \(A_i\);
426	* a triangle using a vertex of \(A_i\), but no \(B_i\), would require adjacent core vertices of the same type.
427	
428	Now suppose there were a \(5\)-cycle.
429	
430	If it used a vertex of \(B_i\), it would contain a segment \(A_i-B_i-A_i\). The remaining \(3\)-edge path between these two \(A_i\)-vertices would have to use an edge between core vertices of type \(i\), which is impossible.
431	
432	Assume therefore that it uses no \(B_i\).
433	
434	* With no \(A_i\)-vertex, it lies in the core, which has girth at least \(9\).
435	* With exactly one \(A_i\)-vertex, its remaining part is a \(3\)-walk in the core between vertices of type \(i\). Their labels are disjoint by (4), so they cannot have this common \(A_i\)-neighbor.
436	* With two \(A\)-vertices, the core vertex between them forces both to belong to the same \(A_i\). The remaining core edge then has endpoints of type \(i\), again impossible.
437	
438	Thus \(G_t\) contains neither a triangle nor a \(5\)-cycle.
439	
440	### 2.4 It cannot map to \(H\)
441	
442	Suppose \(f:G_t\to H\) were a homomorphism. Restrict \(f\) to the original vertices of \(F\).
443	
444	For each \(uv\in E(F)\), the subdivided edge is a \(3\)-walk from \(u\) to \(v\). If \(f(u)=f(v)\), its image would be a closed \(3\)-walk in \(H\), and hence a triangle. Therefore \(f(u)\ne f(v)\).
445	
446	So this restriction is a proper coloring of \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors, contradicting (3).
447	
448	Since \(H\) was arbitrary, every \(c<1/9\) fails.
449	
450	## 3. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
451	
452	Fix \(c>1/9\). Choose small \(d,\varepsilon>0\) such that
453	\[
454	d>\varepsilon,\qquad
455	c-d-2\varepsilon>0,\qquad
456	9c-3d-24\varepsilon>1. \tag{7}
457	\]
458	For example, with \(g=c-1/9\), take \(d=g\) and \(\varepsilon=g/100\).
459	
460	Let \(G\) be \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free with
461	\[
462	\delta(G)\ge cn.
463	\]
464	For sufficiently large \(n\), apply degree-form regularity.
465	
466	Let \(R\) be the reduced graph on \([k]\): \(ij\in E(R)\) precisely when the corresponding pair in \(G'\) is nonempty and regular with density at least \(d\).
467	
468	For any \(v\in V_i\),
469	\[
470	d_{G'}(v)\le |V_0|+m\,d_R(i).
471	\]
472	Consequently,
473	\[
474	m\delta(R)\ge(c-d-2\varepsilon)n>0. \tag{8}
475	\]
476	In particular, \(R\) has no isolated vertices.
477	
478	For a vertex \(x\in V(G)\), define its support
479	\[
480	A(x)=\{i\in[k]:|N_G(x)\cap V_i|\ge2\varepsilon m\}. \tag{9}
481	\]
482	
483	### 3.1 Three consequences of regularity and the forbidden cycles
484	
485	We will use:
486	\[
487	\begin{array}{ll}
488	\text{(a)}&A(x)\text{ is independent in }R;\\[2mm]
489	\text{(b)}&xy\in E(G)\Longrightarrow
490	N_R(A(x))\cap N_R(A(y))=\varnothing
491	\text{ and }A(x)\cap A(y)=\varnothing;\\[2mm]
492	\text{(c)}&x-y-z\text{ a \(2\)-edge path}\Longrightarrow
493	E_R(A(x),A(z))=\varnothing.
494	\end{array} \tag{10}
495	\]
496	
497	Here \(E_R(P,Q)=\varnothing\) means no edge of \(R\) has one endpoint in \(P\) and the other in \(Q\).
498	
499	For clarity, these implications follow directly from the definition of regularity. In an \(\varepsilon\)-regular pair of density at least \(d>\varepsilon\):
500	
501	* two subsets, one on either side and each of size at least \(2\varepsilon m\), have an edge between them;
502	* for a subset of size at least \(2\varepsilon m\) on one side, all but at most \(\varepsilon m\) vertices on the other side have a neighbor in it.
503	
504	Thus:
505	
506	* an edge inside \(A(x)\) would produce a triangle through \(x\), proving (a);
507	* a common reduced neighbor of \(A(x)\) and \(A(y)\) produces a walk
508	  \[
509	  x-a-r-b-y.
510	  \]
511	  If \(xy\) is an edge, this closes to a \(5\)-walk, proving the first assertion of (b);
512	* if \(A(x)\cap A(y)\ne\varnothing\), a neighbor in \(R\) of an index in that intersection is a common reduced neighbor. Such a neighbor exists by (8). This proves the other assertion of (b);
513	* an edge between \(A(x)\) and \(A(z)\), together with \(x-y-z\), produces a closed \(5\)-walk, proving (c).
514	
515	Repeated vertices cause no difficulty: (1) excludes closed odd walks, not just injective cycles.
516	
517	### 3.2 Remove boundedly many wide classes
518	
519	For every \(i\), the set
520	\[
521	\{x:|N_G(x)\cap V_i|>m/2\}
522	\]
523	is wide, by the preliminary observation.
524	
525	Assign every vertex satisfying one or more of these inequalities to the first such index. This gives disjoint wide classes
526	\[
527	D_1,\ldots,D_k,
528	\]
529	some possibly empty. Call their vertices special.
530	
531	For each remaining vertex \(x\),
532	\[
533	|N_G(x)\cap V_i|\le m/2
534	\quad\text{for every }i.
535	\]
536	Using (9),
537	\[
538	\begin{aligned}
539	cn
540	&\le d_G(x)\\
541	&\le |V_0|+|A(x)|\,\frac m2+2\varepsilon km\\
542	&\le3\varepsilon n+|A(x)|\,\frac m2.
543	\end{aligned}
544	\]
545	Hence
546	\[
547	m|A(x)|\ge2(c-3\varepsilon)n. \tag{11}
548	\]
549	In particular, \(A(x)\ne\varnothing\).
550	
551	Partition all nonspecial vertices according to their support \(A(x)\). Together with the nonempty \(D_i\), these form a base partition with at most
552	\[
553	p=k+2^k \tag{12}
554	\]
555	classes.
556	
557	Every base class is independent. This is already true for the \(D_i\); for a support class it follows from (10b) and the nonemptiness of the support.
558	
559	### 3.3 Refine by neighbor signatures
560	
561	Refine each base class according to the set of base classes in which a vertex has at least one neighbor.
562	
563	There are at most
564	\[
565	p2^p \tag{13}
566	\]
567	refined classes.
568	
569	Let \(Q\) be their quotient graph: two distinct refined classes are adjacent if some edge of \(G\) joins them. Since base classes are independent, this is a loopless graph, and the class map is a homomorphism \(G\to Q\).
570	
571	I claim that \(Q\) is triangle-free.
572	
573	Suppose its refined classes \(X,Y,Z\) formed a triangle.
574	
575	**First suppose that \(X\) lies in a special base class \(D_i\).** Choose an actual edge \(yz\) between \(Y\) and \(Z\). Because signatures are constant on refined classes, both \(y\) and \(z\) have a neighbor in \(D_i\). Thus there is a \(3\)-walk with both endpoints in \(D_i\), contradicting its wideness.
576	
577	**Now suppose all three classes are nonspecial.** Write their supports as \(A,B,C\).
578	
579	By (10b), the sets \(A,B,C\) are pairwise disjoint, as are
580	\[
581	N_R(A),\quad N_R(B),\quad N_R(C). \tag{14}
582	\]
583	
584	The neighbor-signature refinement also ensures that a vertex in \(X\) has a neighbor of support \(B\) and a neighbor of support \(C\). Applying (10c) to this \(2\)-edge path shows that \(B\) and \(C\) are anticomplete in \(R\). Cyclically, \(A,B,C\) are pairwise anticomplete. Each is itself independent by (10a).
585	
586	It follows that these six sets are pairwise disjoint:
587	\[
588	A,\ B,\ C,\ N_R(A),\ N_R(B),\ N_R(C). \tag{15}
589	\]
590	
591	Each of the first three has, by (11), size times \(m\) at least \(2(c-3\varepsilon)n\). Each of the last three has, by nonemptiness and (8), size times \(m\) at least \((c-d-2\varepsilon)n\). Therefore
592	\[
593	\begin{aligned}
594	km
595	&\ge m\bigl(
596	|A|+|B|+|C|+
597	|N_R(A)|+|N_R(B)|+|N_R(C)|
598	\bigr)\\
599	&\ge
600	3\bigl(2(c-3\varepsilon)+(c-d-2\varepsilon)\bigr)n\\
601	&=(9c-3d-24\varepsilon)n\\
602	&>n,
603	\end{aligned}
604	\]
605	contradicting \(km\le n\).
606	
607	This proves that \(Q\) is triangle-free.
608	
609	### 3.4 One target works for all inputs
610	
611	Regularity bounds \(k\) by a constant \(K\) depending only on \(c\). Hence (12)–(13) bound \(|V(Q)|\) by a constant depending only on \(c\).
612	
613	Choose an integer \(M\) at least this bound and at least the regularity threshold \(n_0\). Let \(H_c\) be the disjoint union of one copy of every triangle-free graph on at most \(M\) vertices.
614	
615	This is a finite triangle-free graph.
616	
617	* Large input graphs map to their triangle-free quotient \(Q\), which appears in \(H_c\).
618	* Every smaller input graph is itself triangle-free and appears in \(H_c\).
619	
620	Thus every \(c>1/9\) has the required property.
621	
622	Combining the two halves establishes the claimed infimum.
623	
624	## 4. Executed Python checks
625	
626	The following code performs genuine checks, rather than merely printing the proposed answer. It:
627	
628	1. checks the wide-set assertions on every \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph of order at most seven;
629	2. constructs explicit lower-bound graphs and checks the absence of triangles and \(5\)-cycles;
630	3. checks small Kneser chromatic numbers with Z3;
631	4. checks the core’s same-type \(3\)-walk label condition;
632	5. checks the six-set packing implication with Z3;
633	6. verifies exact lower-bound parameter arithmetic for implicit examples approaching \(1/9\).
634	
635	The infinite arguments are proved above; finite experiments are not being substituted for the regularity lemma or Kneser’s theorem.
636	
637	```python

639	from fractions import Fraction
640	from math import comb
641	
642	import networkx as nx
643	import numpy as np
644	import sympy as sp
645	import z3
646	
647	
648	def adjacency(G):
649	    return nx.to_numpy_array(G, nodelist=list(G), dtype=np.int64)
650	
651	
652	def no_C3_C5(G):
653	    # A closed odd walk of length 3 or 5 exists exactly when
654	    # there is an odd cycle of length at most 5.
655	    A = adjacency(G)
656	    A2 = A @ A
657	    A3 = A2 @ A
658	    return np.trace(A3) == 0 and np.trace(A3 @ A2) == 0
659

663	    col = {v: z3.Int("v_" + str(i)) for i, v in enumerate(G)}
664	    solver.add(*[
665	        z3.And(0 <= col[v], col[v] < q) for v in G
666	    ])
667	    solver.add(*[
668	        col[u] != col[v] for u, v in G.edges()
669	    ])
